through_line: Instructions are a supply chain now. MCP can now ship skills, the instruction files that teach an agent to use a server's tools, and today's reads show both halves: how hosts are meant to verify them, and how a skill file can hide commands a reviewer will never see. A Google post and the fork-and-flush study make a similar point about scale: checking work and resetting context matter as much as writing it.

sections.sub: Background reading, not news. Shown with the year it was published.

items.title: Why SELECT * gets slow once JSON columns pass 2 KB
items.summary: Postgres squeezes each row into a quarter of an 8 KB page; anything bigger gets compressed, then moved out to a side table in chunks (TOAST). A 1M-row benchmark shows the cost: compressed values about 2x slower to query, out-of-line ones about 5x, and plain JSON far worse than JSONB. That is the hidden price of selecting a big column you never read.

also.title: pganalyze: Postgres performance cliffs with large JSONB values and TOAST

items.title: MCP servers can now ship the manual for their own tools
items.summary: A walk through the new MCP Skills extension (SEP-2640): each file of a SKILL.md folder becomes a resource, listed with a SHA-256 digest, and the host fetches files only when a task needs them. The worked example puts lazy loading about 22x cheaper across twelve servers. Most of the post is the threat model: remote skills are untrusted text, approval is tied to every file's digest, and any changed file means asking again.

items.title: Hiding a backdoor in a skill that passes human review
items.summary: A security researcher hides instructions in a real, curated skill using invisible Unicode tag characters. A reviewer sees nothing, but the model reads them and runs a shell command. It covers why a skill's name and description are already in the prompt before it is ever used, why agents can write new skills for themselves, and a small scanner that flags long runs of hidden characters.

also.title: Cloud Security Alliance: SKILL.md and the new AI supply-chain attack surface

items.title: Compaction keeps agents in a rut; fresh branches get them out
items.summary: A practitioner unpacks the new Fork-and-Flush paper. Agents running for days settle into one 'idea basin' even with periodic summarising. Splitting into four branches that keep the files but start with an empty chat lifted scores 66% over a single run at equal compute. The ablation is the useful bit: clearing alone or branching alone each gave only part of the gain. It ends with rules: write decisions to files, and rotate rather than compact.

also.title: The paper: Fork-and-Flush, Escaping Idea Basins in Autoresearch Agents

items.title: How Anthropic cut reasoning stolen by distillers 10-100x
items.summary: Training a model on another model's full reasoning traces is what makes copying it work: in their test, a model trained on full traces scored 80.4% on SWE-bench Verified against 71.8% on summarised ones. The post walks through defences that failed and what replaced them: reasoning that cannot be edited or carried between accounts, a two-stage classifier with under 0.1% false positives, and stricter limits for repeat offenders. It is open about the cost to normal users.

items.title: Google's agentic reviewer splits a paper up and checks each part
items.summary: AI conference submissions went from about 23,000 in 2023 to over 74,000 this year, and human review has not kept up. Deep Review's answer is a four-step pipeline: cut the document into parts, give more compute to the dense parts like proofs, check each part in parallel with the whole document in view, then a final agent checks the parts agree. It now takes design docs too.

items.title: Four ways to ask more of a model than faster typing
items.summary: An engineering lead on Claude splits ambition into speed, altitude, depth and range, with prompts for each. Altitude means asking for the outcome, like 'keep the app crash-free' instead of 'fix this crash', and then building the access that makes it possible. Depth means making the model use the methods experts use and getting an outside check, not self-grading. Range means bringing in other fields' methods, not role-play.

items.title: Sapienz, ten years on: from crash-hunting to agent testers
items.summary: A short note on why a 2016 testing paper won an impact award. Sapienz searched app behaviour for three things at once: explore more screens, find more crashes, and keep the steps to reproduce short. It found 558 unknown crashes in 1,000 apps and now runs millions of tests a day at Meta. The ending is the interesting part: the same ideas are now being handed to LLM agents that judge whether behaviour looks right, not just whether it crashed.

also.title: The 2018 deep dive: Sapienz, intelligent automated testing at scale

items.title: TLA+ finds a two-crash data bug hiding in Postgres failover
items.summary: A war story from Supabase's Postgres HA work. Two quick crashes let two standbys promote to the same timeline number separately. pg_rewind sees matching numbers, skips the rewind, and a node quietly keeps writes nobody else has. The TLA+ model is a few hundred lines with an 11-line invariant, and the model checker found the bug after about 7,000 states. The fix is a UUID per promotion.
